title: A Jataka of your choosing
hook: pick one Jataka and read it whole
tomorrow: a bodhisattva is named for hearing. hearing what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Milinda's chariot: a chariot of parts, no fixed core, always repairable. Today, the last of the Pali sources: a tale of your choosing. Today's pick is a hare.
screen: `A CHARIOT OF PARTS.` → `A TALE OF YOUR CHOOSING.`

segments.voice: Stare at a full moon long enough and a picture shows up. Some people see a face. In some places people see a rabbit, and there's a Jataka that explains how it got there. The question it asks is old and plain: what do you give a guest when you have nothing? The hare in this story has only grass. And he still finds something to give.
screen: `A PICTURE IN THE MOON.` → `NOTHING TO GIVE A GUEST.` → `ONLY GRASS.`

segments.voice: The Jatakas are tales of the Buddha's earlier lives. In this one he's a hare in a forest with three friends, a monkey, a jackal and an otter. On a holy day they agree to give food to anyone who asks. The otter finds fish, the jackal finds meat, the monkey brings mangoes. The hare eats grass, and nobody offers a guest grass. So he decides: if anyone asks, I'll give myself. The god Sakka comes, disguised as a hungry brahmin. The hare asks him to build a fire, shakes his fur three times so no insect in it will die, and leaps in. The fire is cold. Not one hair burns. Sakka paints the hare on the moon for everyone to see, and the tale ends the way Jatakas do, naming who was who: the hare was the Buddha himself. That's the teaching. Buddhists hold that awakening grew from many lives of practice, and each Jataka shows one perfection. Here it's dana, giving, at its fullest. A neighbor tradition tells a guest story too. In Genesis, Abraham sits at his tent in the heat, sees three strangers, and in the JPS 1917 words, "he ran to meet them from the tent door." Jewish tradition calls this hachnasat orchim, welcoming guests. Both stories give a stranger everything at hand. The difference is real: Abraham gives from his flock and table, and his guests bring God's promise of a son. The hare has only himself, and his gift is one step on a road of many lives.
screen: `FISH, MEAT, MANGOES, AND GRASS.` · `HE LEAPS. THE FIRE IS COLD.` · `DANA: GIVING, AT ITS FULLEST.` · `ABRAHAM RUNS TO MEET THEM.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN TALE.`

segments.voice: Let the hare's story replay slowly: the friends, the grass, the fire, the moon. Then ask yourself what you have that's yours to give, not money, something like time, attention or a meal, and let one person come to mind who could use it. Rest with them in view.

howItsDone: Jataka tales are retold in sermons, children's books and temple paintings, and some Buddhists see the hare in the moon as a reminder of this tale of giving.

chat.says: ông keeps apologizing he has nothing to give me for the summer. i want him. how do i say that?

chat.meaning: In the Jataka, the hare had only grass, so he offered himself. Giving what is truly yours is the whole gift.

notes: Jataka 316 paraphrased: the four friends, the holy (uposatha) day, the otter's fish, the jackal's meat, the monkey's mangoes, the hare's grass; Sakka disguised as a brahmin; the hare shaking his fur three times to spare insects; the cold fire; the hare painted on the moon; the identification of the hare as the Buddha. Confirm details (the jackal's food is sometimes given as meat and curd).

Unity thread (wisdom day): shared, a stranger who turns out to be holy, welcomed with everything at hand (Genesis 18:2 quoted from JPS 1917, a phrase identical in KJV; Jewish tradition's hachnasat orchim, Shabbat 127a cited as background, not voiced); difference, Abraham gives from his flock and table and his guests bring the promise of a son, while the hare has only himself and his gift is one step on a road of many lives. No ranking; not 'the same'. Keeper (and a Jewish reader) to confirm fairness and the transliteration.
Confirm the JPS 1917 wording of Genesis 18:2 ('he ran to meet them from the tent door').
'Buddhists hold that awakening grew from many lives of practice' and 'each Jataka shows one perfection' are general statements of the Jataka tradition; confirm the phrasing.
